html: In order for a design to come together as uniformly as it does, and for our perceptional take on it to read as good, this is made possible thanks to the 13 Principles of Design. When used right, they will elevate the overall composition of any graphic based design that you are creating.

html:
Principle #1: Contrast

You'll often hear as a designer, the #1 complaint of a client being "Can you make it pop more?" This response is almost always certainly a hint at the fact that what your design needs to have more of, is contrast.

This refers to how different elements are in a design, particularly adjacent elements. When applied right, it makes the right elements stand out. Using differences in color, value, or size to create visual tension and highlight important information. Insufficient contrast can make text content in particular very difficult to read, especially for people with visual impairments.

While contrasting colors are a common way to emphasize contrast, you can also apply it by using different sizes, textures, shapes, weights, and alignment of elements in designs—for example, the color red against a white background or a large, bold font for a call to action.

html:
Principle #2: Balance

All design elements and principles—typography, colors, images, shapes, patterns, etc.—carry a visual weight. Some elements are heavy and draw the eye, while others are lighter. The way these elements are laid out on a page should create a feeling of balance.

There are two basic types of balance: symmetrical and asymmetrical. Symmetrical designs lay out elements of equal weight on either side of an imaginary center line. Asymmetrical balance uses elements of differing weights, often arranged in relation to a line that is not centered within the overall design.

Principle #3: Emphasis

Emphasis is meant to represent the parts of the design that is meant to standout the most purposefully. It's used to direct the viewer to the most important information in the design first. The best way to do this is to use other graphic design best practices and techniques, like color, contrast, white space, or proportion, to make your most important visual elements stand out.

Principle #4: Proportions

Understanding this principle is almost innate to us as human beings, in it's simplest form, this has to do with the size of elements in relation to one another. While it covers that aspect, it also looks at the weight of the design elements. Maintaining proportion creates a visually pleasing balance between objects and is a great way to establish visual hierarchy, as large objects are naturally seen as more important.

Principle #5: Hierarchy

This principle is a strategic in how it handles arranging and emphasizing elements in order of importance. This helps viewers understand your content and quickly directs them to the most important information. This is a principle of design that directly relates to how well content can be processed by people using a website. Hierarchy is most easily illustrated through the use of titles and headings in a design. 

The title of a page should be given the most importance, and therefore should be immediately recognizable as the most important element on a page; whereas headings and subheadings should be formatted in a way that shows their importance in relation to each other as well as in relation to the title and body copy.

Principle #6: Repetition

This principle looks at the emphasis of a design with reusing similar or the same elements throughout the design. It is a great way to reinforce an idea or unify a design that brings together alot of different elements. Repetition can also help establish your brand identity to create memorable and impactful designs through repeated elements in a specified layout. The principle of repetition is even present in how we structure and represent this page, having an image on the left for one, and then in the other, the image is on the right, and continuously alternated creating that repetition.

Principle #7: Rhythm

Rhythm creates a sense of movement, flow, and visual interest within designs. It’s similar to repetition but focuses on the placement and spacing between the repeated elements.

There are four types of rhythm you can apply to graphic designs:


Regular rhythm uses the same clear pattern and spacing between repeated elements.

Random rhythm follows no distinct pattern, and elements are placed at random.

Flowing rhythm creates movement and fluidity by repeating elements in a curved pattern using lines and organic shapes.

Progressive rhythm subtly changes each repeated element to show a gradual progression.

Principle #8: Pattern

Pattern is repeating multiple structured elements together to form a cohesive design. While pattern and repetition are closely linked, the core difference lies in their structure and complexity: repetition is simply using the same element multiple times to create consistency, whereas a pattern is a highly structured, predictable sequence created by combining multiple repeating elements.
